sourceLines.text: How do you take your 1,3,7-Trimethylpurine-2,6-dione? In a cappuccino, perhaps,
or a nice cup of tea? If you’re a student, you might take it in Red Bull, especially
at exam times, and those with a sweet tooth might prefer to take it in chocolate.
Here  are  some  statistics:  90%  of  all  adults  on  the  planet  consume  1,3,7-
Trimethylpurine-2,6-dione  every day,  with 1,3,7-Trimethylpurine-2,6-dione drunk
in  2.25  billion cups  of  coffee.  That’s  not  counting  all  the  Pepsis,  Coca-Colas,
chocolates and energy drinks, which also contain 1,3,7-Trimethylpurine-2,6-dione.
120,000 tonnes of this naturally-occurring substance are consumed every year. It is
the world’s most commonly used drug.
1,3,7-Trimethylpurine-2,6-dione is a bit of a mouthful, so let’s call it by its more
common name: caffeine. Found in the seed of the coffee plant, the leaf of the tea
bush, the cocoa bean and in the kola nut, it functions as a natural pesticide since it
is poisonous to insects that attempt to feed on these plants.
So  when  did  people  start  to  consume  this  substance?  According  to  legend,  the
Emperor  Shennong,  who  reigned  in  China  around  3,000  BCE,  accidentally
discovered tea when certain leaves fell into boiling water. He found that when the
leaves  were  left  to  boil,  a  fragrant  drink  resulted.  The  earliest  record  of  coffee
consumption occurs in the mid-fifteenth century, in the Yemeni city of Mocha. Not
many Westerners know that  mocha comes from Mocha, but it was from here that
coffee spread to the rest of the Middle East and then Europe. As for the consumption
of caffeine in the kola nut, kola nuts have been chewed in West Africa for thousands
of years.  Finally,  the  first  historical  evidence  of  the  consumption  of  caffeine  in
cocoa  nuts  occurs  in  South  America,  with  residues  found  in  an  ancient  Mayan
cooking pot dating from 600 BCE. The Mayans made a drink using cocoa, which
they called Xocolatl, and when the Spanish conquered the Mayan Empire they added
sugar to it and called it chocolate.
We all know the basic effects of caffeine consumption: it wakes you up and gives
you  energy,  but  what  of  the  health  effects?  Here  the  results  are  very  definitely
mixed,  and  depend  largely  on  the  scale  of  consumption.  Studies  suggest  that
consumption of 3 to 5 cups of coffee per day may protect against certain diseases,
including Parkinson’s disease, some types of cancer, and heart disease. However,
the risk of heart disease and strokes  increases with consumption of more than 5
cups per day. Some people’s sleep patterns are disturbed by caffeine consumption
but  others’  are  not.  Finally,  consumption  of  caffeine  in  coffee  is  definitely  not
recommended for pregnant women.
________________  (See  question  10.)  Perhaps  the  next  time  you’re  in  KFUPM
Mall,  or  you  go  to  Joffrey’s,  don’t  ask  for  coffee.  Ask  for  some  1,3,7-
Trimethylpurine-2,6-dione instead, and see how they react.

Smartphone Addiction and Its Harmful Effects
Smartphones: Their Advantages and Disadvantages
The Global Popularity of Mobile Devices

sourceLines.text: Globally, about 5.13 billion people own mobile devices,
most  of  which  are  classified  as  smartphones.  That  is
roughly two-thirds of the population of our planet. And
this prevalence has introduced a mental health condition
unique to the 21 st century: smartphone addiction. We all
Does this remind you of anyone?
recognise the traits of smartphone addicts. They are those
individuals  who  cannot  or  will  not  put  away  their  smartphones,  even  when  their
continued  use  is  grotesquely  inappropriate,  for  example,  when  driving  a  car,  or
studying in a classroom.  They are those people who wake up in the middle of the
night to check their phones, or who feel anxious when they can’t get to their phones,
or  whose  phone  use  impacts  negatively  on  work  performance,  education  or
relationships. Compulsive use of smartphones, it seems, has replaced caffeine as the
world’s most common addiction.
________________  (See  question  3.)  Amongst  medical  professionals,  there  is
discussion over whether phone overuse should be classified as such. On the one hand,
in  contrast  to  behaviors  commonly  recognized  as  addictions,  smoking,  or  illegal
narcotics, there is no ingestion of chemicals. Those overusing their smartphones are
not eating, drinking or smoking anything. In this case, it is better classified as a
behavioral  issue,  rather  than  addiction.  On  the  other  hand,  some  medical
professionals  compare  smartphone  overuse  to  gambling  addiction.  They  point  to
dopamine,  a  chemical  produced  in  the  brain,  which,  when
released, makes you feel good. Gambling leads to the release of
dopamine,  and  so,  they  argue,  does  smartphone  use.  It  is  the
dopamine which is addictive. Using a smartphone is a way of
ensuring its release. Of whether it is a genuine addiction I am
Gambling Addiction unsure.  However,  we  all  know  that  it  is  something real,  and
something bad, because we see it every day.
But smartphone addiction isn’t doing any real harm,
is it? Tell that to your teacher.  Over the last 20 years,
those working in education have seen at first hand the
damage  smartphone  addiction  has  done  to  students.
Or  rather,  the  damage  students  have  done  to
themselves. Students who fail courses are often those
who  just  cannot  put  their  smartphones  away.  Apart
from being rude and disrespectful to their teachers,
those  on  their  phones  in  class  are  dividing  their
attention  between  their  studies,  and  whatever  is  on Is This Doing Anybody Any Good?
their phones.  They learn less. Teachers regularly witness students racing through
exercises, without taking anything in, just so they can get back to their smartphones.
Education suffers. Life chances suffer. It is wrong and it is a waste.
But nobody’s dying from it, right? Wrong. Figures released by the UK’s Department
of Transport show that in 2016 drivers using mobiles were responsible for 308 minor
injuries, 90 serious injuries and 33 fatalities. In the US, the National Safety Council
reports that phone use while driving leads to 1.6 million crashes each year, with up
to 390,000 injuries from accidents caused by texting while driving. 25% of all car
accidents in the US are caused by texting while driving. Smartphones are literally
causing people to die.

options.text: California’s Most Important Cities
Is it Possible to Predict Earthquakes?
What Are The Worst Kinds of Natural Disasters?
The 1906 San Francisco Earthquake and Fire

sourceLines.text: San  Francisco,  Wednesday,  April  18,  1906.  The  earthquake  struck  at  05:12  am
Pacific Time. With a magnitude estimated at from 7.7 to 8.3 on the Richter scale
and  an  epicentre  located  offshore  at  37.75°N,  122.55°W,  3  kilometres  west  of
Ocean Beach, it brought destruction along 476 kilometres of the San Andreas Fault.
Seismic  waves  moved  at  speeds  of  22,000  kilometres  per  hour.  High-intensity
shaking  was  felt  from  as  far  north  as  Oregon  to  as  far  south  as  Los  Angeles.
Preceded by a strong foreshock by about 20 to 25 seconds, the quake itself lasted
approximately 42 seconds. It destroyed 80% of the city of San Francisco. During
the quake, and in the fire that raged during its aftermath, 3,000 people are believed
to  have  died,  and,  out  of  a  total  population  of  410,000,  between  227,000  and
300,000 lost their homes. It remains the greatest natural disaster in the history of
California.
_______________ (See the appropriate question.) The inferno raged for four days,
from Montgomery Street to Chinatown, and between North Beach and Telegraph
Hill, until finally extinguished by rain. In the process, it had destroyed 500 city
blocks, an area of 10 square kilometres, levelling some 28,000 buildings. The total
property  value  loss  was  estimated  at  $350  million  dollars,  equivalent  to  $7.67
billion in 2021 values. Those same experts identify three causal factors behind the
strength of the fire.
Firstly, the earthquake damaged much of the city’s gas mains infrastructure. Gas
leaks from ruptured pipes led to over 30 fires, which then merged to create a city-
destroying inferno. Secondly, the San Francisco Fire Department attempted to limit
the  spread  of  the  conflagration  by  creating  fire-breaks.  They  did  this  by  using
explosives to destroy buildings that stood in the direction of travel of the fire.
Unfortunately, the department’s chief expert in the use of explosives, Dennis T
Sullivan, had been killed in the first seconds of the earthquake. The firefighters,
inexperienced in the use of explosives, did not create effective fire-breaks, but
actually made the situation worse by setting fire to many buildings. Finally, home
insurance policies belonging to home owners in San Francisco and its suburbs did
not cover damage by earthquakes. They did, however, cover damage by fires. Home
owners the earthquake damage to whose homes would have left them in poverty set
fires to their own homes so they could claim on the insurance.
And of the aftermath? At the time, San Francisco was the ninth largest city in the
United States, and the largest city in California. Following the disaster, although
it rebuilt quickly, trade, industry and population growth was diverted south to Los
Angeles, which during the 20 th century became the West’s most important urban
area. As of May 2021, its rank has slipped to the 16 th most populous city in the
United States, and California’s fourth, with a population of 881.549.
As for the earthquake survivors, in 2006, the centenary commemorations in 2006
were attended by eleven, including Irma Mae Weule (May 11, 1899 – August 8,
2008)  and  Vivian  Illing  (December  25,  1900  –  January  22,  2009.)  Since  that
centenary  events,  however,  more  survivors  have  been  found,  including  William
Del Monte, who lived from January 22, 1906 to January 11, 2016. He died 11 days
short of his 110 th birthday, the last survivor of the Great San Francisco Earthquake
of Wednesday, April 18, 1906.

options.text: A Step on The Journey to Mars
Gravity: The Science of Satellites
The International Space Station
The World’s Biggest Space Agencies

sourceLines.text: The International Space Station (ISS) is a habitable
artificial  satellite  in  low  Earth  orbit.  Resulting
from the participation of 5 separate space agencies
(the  United  States’  NASA,  Russia’s  Roscosmos,
Japan’s  JAXA,  Europe’s  ESA  and  the  Canadian
CSA), it developed from a 1984 American proposal
to construct a permanently-manned modular Earth-
orbiting satellite.
The  ISS’s  first  module  was  launched  on  20 The ISS
November 1998 from the Baikonur Cosmodrome, a Russian spaceport located in
Kazakhstan.  Since  that  time,  it  has  grown  to  include  16  separate  pressurized
modules. With a current length of 73 metres, a width of 109 metres and a mass of
419,725 kilograms, it contains a pressurised volume of 915.6 cubic metres. Power
and electricity are sourced from two solar arrays containing numerous photovoltaic
cells. These are 375 metres in area, and track the Sun to maximise power generation.
The ISS carries a crew of 7. As the largest manmade object in space, it is frequently
visible to the naked eye, and, at an accumulated total cost (by 2010) of $150 billion
dollars, it is by far the single most expensive object ever built.
The  ISS  does  not  exist  in  conditions  of  zero  gravity.  Gravity  is  at  a  level
approximately 90% of Earth’s, but the ISS’s movement creates a weightlessness
identical to that of zero gravity. The ISS is in constant freefall towards the surface
of Earth: due to the curvature of the Earth, however, its velocity ensures that the
distance  to  the  surface  remains  almost  constant.  The  velocity  required  is  7.66
kilometres per second, or 27,576 kilometres per hour. Over time, the ISS’s altitude
falls as the result of orbital decay. The ISS is in low Earth orbit, and there are still
atmospheric gases, which creates drag on the ISS and causes its velocity to fall
slightly.  As  its  velocity  falls,  its  altitude  falls  (at  a  rate  of  approximately  4
kilometres a month) until it reaches its perigee altitude of 418 kilometres. At this
point,  it  fires  its  thrusters  to  increase  velocity,  and  this  allows  it  to  regain  its
apogee altitude of 422 kilometres. The ISS orbits the Earth 16 times every day. As
of December 2020, it had orbited the Earth 125,964 times.
______________  (See  the  appropriate  question.)  According  to  the  1988
agreement signed between the participating space agencies, the ISS was intended
to  provide  a  platform  and  environment  in  which  to  conduct  experiments  and
research that could only be done in space. This has thus far included scientific work
from a diverse field of subjects, including astrobiology, meteorology and medical
science.  Another  of  the  ISS’s  stated  purposes  was  to  conduct  research  into  the
viability of manned missions to Mars, although it is not currently clear as to what
extent this objective has been realised. The most significant of the scientific work
carried  out  on  the  ISS  has  probably  been  that  using  the  Alpha  Magnetic
Spectrometer, the purpose of which is to detect dark matter, and to answer other
fundamental questions about the universe. On 13 April 2013, scientists using the
Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer reported an incredible discovery.

sourceLines.text: In the years 1816 to 1820, the British landscape artist J. M. W. Turner (1775 – 1851)
produced the works for which he is best known. His renderings of the landscapes of
London at sunset are famous for the spectacular shades of orange and red with which
he depicted the sky, colours quite unlike anything that would have normally been
seen.  Now,  scientists  have  realised  that  these  colours  were  not  drawn  from  his
imagination. These intense colours, Turner’s famous blood-red London sunsets, were
the direct result of an event that had taken place at a distance of 12,639 kilometres
from  London.  They  were  one  aspect  of  a  natural  disaster  which  impacted
devastatingly on the global climate in 1816.
Mount Tambura is an active volcano located on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa.
On 10th April 1815, following several weeks of warning signs including the emissions
of palls of black smoke and explosions, it erupted. Registering 7 on the VEI index,
a unit of measurement similar to that used to measure earthquakes, its explosion was
heard  in  the  city  of  Jakarta,  1,260  kilometres  away.  Before  the  eruption,  Mount
Tambura had a height of 4,300 metres, and was one of the highest mountains on any
of the islands of the Indonesian archipelago. After the explosion, its height had been
reduced to 2,851 metres. It was the most violent volcanic eruption ever witnessed by
human beings.
________________  (See  question  8.)  Whole  villages  disappeared  forever.  All
vegetation  on  the  island  was  destroyed,  covered  under  a  metre  of  volcanic  ash.
Created by the force of the explosion, tsunamis devastated the coastal regions of
surrounding Indonesian islands. It would be weeks before survivors again saw the
Sun.
However,  it  was  the  eruption’s  aftermath,  particularly  its  impact  on  the  global
climate,  that  was  to  prove  even  more  devastating.  During  the  eruption,  10,000
million tonnes of pyroclastic trachyandesite, along with carbon monoxide, carbon
dioxide and sulphur dioxide, were released. Rising from the volcano, a column of
toxic smoke reached a height of 43 kilometres. These emissions were to change the
composition of the Earth’s atmosphere in the years to come. This is why Turner’s
paintings of London sunsets are so unusual in colour. They also impacted on global
temperatures. The gases released into the atmosphere reduced the amount of heat the
Earth received from the Sun: an event critical for both global temperatures and global
agriculture.
In 1816, global temperature fell by an average of 0.53 °C. It was the coldest year
since the 15 th century, coming to be known as the Year Without A Summer. Freak
weather conditions were experienced worldwide. Blizzards and snow storms were
reported in Canada in June. In China and India, the monsoons, the summer rains, did
not come that year. In Britain, winter temperatures lasted well into May. All of this
was  devastating  for  global  agricultural  production.  In  1816,  there  were  famines
worldwide.  Deaths  from  the  starvation  that  occurred  as  an  indirect  result  of  the
Mount Tambura eruption are now estimated at almost 100,000 people.

sourceLines.text: Vernon Smith, 82, is one of Britain’s most successful writers. A father of three,
he lives in the town of his birth, Drizzley, with his wife Jenny, to whom he has
been  married  for  fifty  years.  Nowadays  internationally  famous  thanks  to  the
runaway  success  of  his  autobiographical  work  My  Childhood,  Vernon  came  to
writing  comparatively  late  in  life,  following  his  retirement  from  the  asbestos
factory  where  he  was  foreman  for  over  sixty  years.  Here  he  describes  the
childhood that was to provide such rich material for his writing.
_________________ (See question 3.) There was Mother, me, and seventeen other
children. When I was two months old, my father died when he was run over by a farm
tractor bringing sheep back from market. If he’d lived, our situation would have been
better but, as it was, our family was left without a breadwinner. Mother did her best.
She’d take in washing or sew for rich ladies, but that was barely enough to pay the
rent. We were eligible for charity, cash hand-outs, but Mother was too proud to accept
that.  ‘We’re  not  common!’  she’d  say.  ‘We’re  not  beggars!’  And  so  we  lived  in
poverty, not that I knew that at the time. If I’d ever seen any money, I’d have known
I didn’t have any. So I had no idea we were poor. I thought everybody on our street
lived like that.
The nineteen of us lived in a two-room house in Drizzley. Hot water? We didn’t have
cold water. Any water would have been a luxury to us. When we needed water, we’d
go down to the canal and bring it back in a bucket. In winter, when the canal had
frozen over, I’d need to break the ice with a rusty hammer before I could get to it.
We had no heating either. The best we could do for heating was to sit round a candle.
We had one meal a day, and it was always a potato, apart from special occasions when
we got a carrot. All the children slept in the kitchen. Me and my brothers slept on top
of the kitchen table, and our sisters slept under it. When I was five, I started school.
It  wasn’t  a  school  for  normal  kids.  It  was  the  Drizzley  Free  School  For  The
Unfortunate Children Of Paupers. It was twenty miles away from our house, and the
teachers would beat us if we were late. I’d get up at four in the morning to walk there
for the start of the school day. It was always raining, apart from when it was snowing.
So that was Vernon’s childhood. How does he feel his childhood compares to the
lives of young people nowadays?
Young people nowadays don’t know they’re born. They think they’re doing badly if
they don’t have the latest Apple iPhone or if they don’t have a new car! They’re all
addicted to their smartphones and they always say they’re bored. I was never bored
as a child. Me and my seventeen brothers and sisters, we made our own fun in those
days. And, looking back, I have to say that my childhood were the happiest days of
my life.

sourceLines.text: Located  in  the  North  of  England,  Yorkshire  is  a  region  with  a
unique identity. Subdivided into four separate administrative areas
(North  Yorkshire,  West  Yorkshire,  South  Yorkshire  and  East
Yorkshire), in 2011 it had a population of 5,288,200 and has an area
of  11,903  square  kilometres.  Famed  not  only  for  its  beautiful
countryside  but  also  its  vibrant  multicultural  cities,  Yorkshire’s
emblem is a white rose on a blue background. Hence its nickname, the Yorkshire
White Rose County.
________________ (See question 3.) Its unique identity, however, possibly stems
more from its invasion and settlement by the Vikings, who established the Viking
Kingdom  of  Jorvik  in  866  CE,  which  formed  Yorkshire’s  present  geographical
boundaries. Although the Kingdom of Jorvik only lasted for 100 years, the Viking
influence  is  still  present.  For  example,  many  words  in  the  Yorkshire  dialect  of
English derive from words in Old Norse. The common Yorkshire greeting eh up! is
of  Viking  origin  (in  present-day  Danish,  eh  op!).  Words  such  as  dale (valley),
beck (river) and bairn (child) are also of Old Norse origin.
For visitors to Yorkshire, the first port of call is usually the historic city of York.
Founded in 71 CE, the city was known as  Eboracum by the Romans, and by the
Vikings as  Jorvik, from which the name  York is derived. A walled city formed at
the confluence of the Ouse and the Foss (which both often flood), no visit to York
would be complete without a visit to the Shambles, the series of medieval streets at
the heart of the city. Yorkshire does, however, have other cities worth a visit. The
industrial  cities  of  Sheffield,  Hull,  Leeds  and  Bradford  all  have  something  of
interest to the visitor, especially Leeds, with its vibrant student life and the famous
football stadium at Elland Road.
For fans of English literature, a visit to the Yorkshire town of Haworth, situated 7
kilometres south of Keighley, is recommended. It was here in the 19 th century that
the Brontës, Emily, Charlotte and Anne, lived, died and wrote their famous novels,
Wuthering Heights, Shirley and  Jane Eyre. You can even visit Haworth’s Brontë
Parsonage, the home where they spent their lives and which now serves as a museum
to the sisters.
Or you can go wandering over the cloudy rain-soaked moors where so many of their
stories were set. Yorkshire is famous for its spectacular moors, wild areas of open
countryside, hills, valleys and rivers. Haworth Moor and Ilkley Moor are both good
places to go walking (if you don’t mind the cold) but the most famous is probably
the  North  Yorkshire  Moor,  a  national  park  of  1,430  square  kilometres  which
stretches all the way to the east coast town of Whitby.
Nowadays, Yorkshire is easier to get to than ever before, with KLM operating a
route from Dammam to Leeds Bradford Airport (via Amsterdam.) With tourism such
big business in Yorkshire, there’s always a huge range of hotels and accommodation
available. If you visit, be prepared for bad weather, though. It rains in autumn. It
rains in winter. It rains in spring. It rains in summer. It rains a lot in Yorkshire, so
bring a raincoat.

options.text: Advice on Doing Reading Exams
Dealing with Exam Failure
Health Problems Resulting from Exam Failure
How Students Feel about Studying at KFUPM

sourceLines.text: Hey you! Yes, YOU! See that big disembodied hand on the left with the
pointy  finger?  Well,  that  finger’s  pointed  directly  at  you.  Not  your
teacher, not the invigilator up at the top desk, not whoever’s sitting next to you or
some dodgy character next door, but  you: a young man or woman, probably Saudi,
studying ENGL04 in the Prep Year right now. You’re reading this as part of Major
Two in 212 FH, and I am talking to you. This whole text is written for you, and it is
written with the hope of giving you advice: how to deal with failure. Now we don’t
expect you to do badly in this test. We want you to do well! But under-performance
in exams is something we don’t often talk about, and I think we should!
________________ (See the appropriate question.) A huge weight of expectation is
placed on students, by families, by friends, by students themselves. Despite what
your teacher or the test-writer may think, it isn’t just another exam. It’s your self-
confidence, your self-esteem, your emotional well-being, your future, your family’s
expectations. When you do poorly in an exam, you can feel you’ve let your family
down. Poor exam performance is linked to depression, anxiety, insomnia and a host
of other neurological conditions. And students who come to KFUPM have often never
failed any exams before; have never, in fact, even had scores that were below average
before. They have always been a breeze, a doddle, something you could do standing
on your head. So it’s no wonder that, when they do poorly, some students give in to
the temptation to respond in inappropriate ways.
Like going to the Program Manager to announce, with zero evidence or justification
but with maximum conviction, that there is a problem with the exam score. That the
OMR needs to be rechecked until, finally, you’re happy with the exam score. Let me
save  everybody  a  little  time  here.  There  is  no  problem  with  the  exam  score.  The
problem, if it can be defined as such, is that the student is not happy with the exam
score,  which is not really a problem. Honestly, rather than bothering the Program
Manager with imaginary problems, the best thing to do is to take it on the chin and
move on.
Or do the following: use failure as an opportunity to learn and grow. It is by our
failures that we reassess our working strategies and improve. It is in the aftermath
of failure that crucial questions are posed:
How could I have done better? 
 How effectively did I manage my time?
 Did I focus on what was necessary?
 What do I need to do to get better next time?
And,  by  asking  yourself  those  questions,  you  are  developing  a  whole  separate
skillset, derived from your original failure but existing independently of it. Failure
brings personal growth. It allows you to develop vital new skills. Without failure,
there is no progress.
A famous man once said success is not final. Failure is not fatal. It is the courage
to continue that counts. And this is true for students in the Prep Year. What should
you be proudest of? Easy success? Or to fail and to fail, and then, through your own
hard work and growth, to pass? It’s not success that gives life meaning: it’s struggle.
Failing exams builds character.

sourceLines.text: On the 13 th of April in the year 1314, in response to complaints by shopkeepers and
merchants  of  the  city  of  London,  King  Edward  the  II  of  England  issued  a
proclamation in which he banned the playing of a certain game. There had been, the
proclamation informed the citizens of London, a great deal of violence associated
with this game, which involved the kicking of a ball through the nets of an opposing
team. Unemployed young men watching or playing this game, which we now know
as  football, had fought each other, causing injury and bringing great disruption to
the city’s shops and markets. From this time on, according to King Edward’s new
law, any young man found playing this game within the city of London was to be
imprisoned.  It  was  the  first  recorded  example  of  a  legal  response  to  football
violence.
________________  (See  question  5.)  It  has  built  bridges  between  nations  and
brought inspiration to millions. However, football also has a dark side. Wherever
and  whenever  it  has  been  played,  it  seems,  violence  has  been  close  by.  Football
violence exists isn so many countries that the same word is used globally to describe
its practitioners:  hooligan. Japanese, Polish, Russian, French and countless other
languages use  hooligan to describe a violent person who fights over football. The
use  of  a  word  derived from  English, which,  when  used in other languages  refers
specifically to a violent football fan, also points to the English origins of football
violence.  England  gave  the  world  football.  Unfortunately,  it  also  gave  the  world
football violence. Even now football violence is often known as the English Disease.
In London on October 26 th 1863, the Football Association was established and the
rules of the modern game were written down for the first time. In 1885, after Preston
North End beat Aston Villa 5-0, players from both teams were beaten with sticks,
punched,  kicked  and  spat  at  by  hooligans.  It  was  the  first  famous  incidence  of
violence in the modern game, but it was not the last. Football violence in Britain has
continued  to  the  present  day,  although  it  reached  its  peak  in  the  1970s  and  80s.
During those decades, large-scale fighting before, during or after matches between
rival firms was common. All the major clubs had firms, whose members would travel
to home and away matches with the intention of fighting, with the worst reputations
belonging  those  of  Leeds  United,  Arsenal  and  Manchester  United.  Nowadays,
however,  a  combination  of  more  effective  policing  and  changing  social  attitudes
means that football violence in the UK is a fraction of what it once was.
If England’s history of football violence is the longest, South America’s is the most
violent. On 24 th April 1964, in Lima, the capital of Peru, 300 fans were killed and
another  500  injured  when  fighting  broke  out  between  rival  supporters  at  a  Peru-
Argentina qualifying match for the Olympic Games. At a match in the Argentine
capital  Buenos  Aires  in  1968,  70  fans  were  killed  during  fighting.  A  2002
government  investigation  into  football  violence  in  Argentina  stated  that  it  was  a
national crisis, with many killed or injured through stabbings or gunshot wounds.

sourceLines.text: What do actors Sean Connery, Kevin Costner, and Russell Crowe
all  have  in  common?  (Considering  how  many  Netflix  movies
people watch, you must have heard of one of these names.) The
answer is that each of these Hollywood superstars has portrayed
a movie version of the English folk hero, Robin Hood.
Do  you  know  the  story  of  Robin  Hood?
He’s an outlaw who robs from the rich to
give  to  the  poor.  He  lives  in  the  time  of
King Richard, in the 12 th century, and lives
in  Sherwood  Forest  with  his  gang  of
outlaws,  the  Merry  Men:  there’s  Little
Sherwood Forest Robin Hood
John,  who’s  very  big,  and  Friar  Tuck,  who’s  very  fat.  Then
there’s Maid Marian, his wife, with whom he’s besotted. Robin is a master archer,
famous for his accuracy with a bow and arrow, and he and the Merry Men are at
loggerheads  with  the  local  ruler,  the  evil  Sheriff  of  Nottingham,  who  is  always
stealing money from the poor of Nottingham, and making their lives a misery. Robin,
on the other hand, is constantly robbing the Sheriff, making  his life a misery, and
giving the money back to the poor.
So how long has the fictional Robin Hood existed within popular culture? He seems
to have originated in oral tradition, featuring in the songs popular during medieval
England’s May Day festivities. The first  written reference to Robin Hood appears
in the poem Piers Plowman, believed to have been composed in the 1370s. This was
the first of many such references. William Shakespeare references Robin Hood twice,
firstly in the Two Gentlemen of Verona, and then in his comedy As You Like It, (first
performed in 1599) when a character says of the Duke that he is already in the forest
of Arden, and a many merry men with him; and there they live like the old Robin
Hood of England. In 1585, the young James VI of Scotland (later James I of England)
was entertained by a Robin Hood Play at Dirleton Castle in Scotland: the intention
was to distract the young king from the horrific plague then ravaging his capital,
Edinburgh.  Following  a  slight  lull  in  the  17 th and  18 th centuries,  the  19 th century
writer Sir Walter Scott re-popularised Robin Hood in his novel Ivanhoe, setting the
stage for Robin Hood’s 20 th and 21st century Golden Age: Robin Hood in Hollywood
movies. Robin has been portrayed on screen by some of Hollywood’s biggest names.
The most recent is Robin Hood (2018) with Taron Egerton in the title role, and Ben
Mendelsohn as the Sheriff of Nottingham. It appears not to have been a success, with
a mediocre rating of 5.3 on imdb.com. That is the story of the fictional Robin Hood.
________________  (See  the  appropriate  question.)  It’s  possible:  historian  David
Crook  believes  he  has  identified  the  historical  figure  behind  the  legend  of  Robin
Hood. There are historical records of a criminal by the name of Robert Wetherby, a
native of Yorkshire, who used the alias Robin Hood, and was in 1225 hunted down
and killed by a posse at the behest of the real sheriff of Nottingham. So, it seems,
amidst all the embellishments there is a tiny bit of truth to the legend of Robin Hood.
